knowledge_fragments.content: Myeloid sarcoma (MS) is a tumor mass composed of myeloid blasts at extramedullary sites. Individual cases of MS exhibit the broad spectrum of differentiation and maturation observed in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Myelomonocytic or monoblastic MS can be positive for CD4, CD68, CD163, and lysozyme, which can also present a potential diagnostic pitfall when distinguishing from HS. The atypical histiocytoid cells of HS tend to be more pleomorphic, while myeloid blasts of MS are smaller and more monotonous (Figure 2E). A history or concurrence of AML and the presence of CD34 or myeloperoxidase expression would suggest a diagnosis of MS. However, monoblastic MS often lacks these expressions.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 53-year-old male patient, with no prior medical history, presented to the emergency department in March 2019 with a 12 kg weight loss over 6 months, fatigue, and a syncopal event. Initial blood tests showed leukocytes at 40 × 10^9/L, neutrophils at 24 × 10^9/L, lymphocytes at 12 × 10^9/L, eosinophils at 3.5 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin at 12.6 g/dL, and platelets at 120 × 10^9/L, with no other abnormalities. A bone marrow biopsy and aspiration were performed, revealing no myeloid or lymphoid blasts. Morphological and immunohistochemical analysis indicated a chronic myeloproliferative condition with a non-specific histological pattern and a mild increase in the reticular network. Further studies conducted between April and August 2019 included a normal karyotype (46XY), unmutated JAK2 V617F, CALR exon 9, and MPL exon 10. During a hematology consultation in December 2019, a new blood cell count showed leukocytes at 14.8 × 10^9/L, neutrophils at 6.5 × 10^9/L, monocytes at 1.65 × 10^9/L, eosinophils at 1.31 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin at 19.3 g/dL, hematocrit at 60%, and platelets at 41 × 10^9/L.. Confirmed diagnosis: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and BCR/FGFR1 rearrange

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: An 11-year-old girl presented with symptoms of blurry vision and progressive loss of vision over the course of one month. Her vision deteriorated rapidly during this period without experiencing headache, increased urination, excessive thirst, or increased hunger. There was no significant change in body weight. Her past medical history was unremarkable, with no history of trauma, radiation exposure, maternal or current infections, or drug use. Ophthalmological examination revealed 20/50 vision in the right eye and 20/66 in the left eye, with diffuse white cortical changes and posterior subcapsular cataract. The pupils reacted normally to light. The fundus oculi was visible after mydriasis. Ultrasonography indicated bilateral cataract without vitreous opacity or retinal detachment. Electrophysiology (ERG) showed slightly reduced amplitudes of a and b waves for the left eye. No abnormalities were detected by fluorescein fundus angiography and visual evoked potentials (VEP) test.. Confirmed diagnosis: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus. Differential diagnosis includes: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.

Laboratory results showed elevated serum cortisol levels. Upon examination at the eye outpatient department, findings included decreased tear meniscus levels and mild superficial punctate keratitis in the superior region of both corneas. The anterior segment examination revealed no other abnormalities. Schirmer test showed less than 5mm of wetting of filter paper after five minutes. Both eyes revealed optic disc pallor temporally confirmed on SD-OCT.. Confirmed diagnosis: Triple-A Syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Triple-A Syndrome.

Because the kinase gene rearrangement is definitional, these leukemias should not be diagnosed as MPAL regardless of the immunophenotype.

Laboratory tests revealed normal levels of haemoglobin, total leukocyte count, liver function, kidney function, and D-dimer.. Confirmed diagnosis: pheochromocytoma. knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 30-year-old female patient presented with elevated haemoglobin levels detected 4 years prior. She had previously undergone bone marrow aspiration and biopsy at a local hospital. Genetic testing using qPCR did not reveal common mutations associated with certain conditions. The initial bone marrow biopsy results were unavailable. The patient received phlebotomy and oral aspirin therapy. Upon visiting our hospital in October 2020, her haemoglobin level was recorded at 198.0 g/L.. Confirmed diagnosis: Myeloproliferative Neoplasm with JAK2 exon12 mutation. Differential diagnosis includes: Myeloproliferative Neoplasm with JAK2 exon12 mutation.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 41-year-old male has experienced erythrocytosis and elevated hematocrit levels for the past 5 years. Initial laboratory tests reveal high hemoglobin (17.8 g/dL) and hematocrit (54%), with normal white blood cell count (6.7 × 10^9/L) and platelet count (203 × 10^9/L). Erythropoietin levels are below the local laboratory reference range (3.9 mU/mL [4.3–29]). A JAK2 mutation with a 2.8% variant allele frequency is identified in peripheral blood granulocytes. knowledge_fragments.content: The main mechanism of pathological leukocytosis is a productive one due to intensified leukopoiesis. It may be neoplastic, i.e., resulting from monoclonal neoplastic proliferation (in leukemias and lymphomas), or reactive (i.e., resulted from polyclonal WBC proliferation in response to some cytokine-mediated stimulation of leukopoiesis). Polyclonal reactive leukocytosis accompanies various infections, inflammatory diseases, and some non-leukemic malignant neoplasms. The aseptic inflammation is also able to render cytokine-mediated stimulation of WBC production; hence, leukocytosis is not always a witness for infection. Allergic reactions; autoimmune diseases; burns, frostbite, and injuries; the disintegration of malignant tumors and the development of myocardial necrosis during infarction; acute onset of radiation sickness; and debut phase of intoxications killing the bone marrow cells, like in uremia, may all cause reactive leukocytosis. Severe dehydration of the organism (like in diabetic coma) causes pathologically false leukocytosis without stimulation of leukopoiesis, due to blood thickening.

knowledge_fragments.content: VEGF, initially known as vascular permeability factor, has a recognized role in the accumulation of ascitic fluid. Several studies have confirmed, using enzyme immunoassay, the presence of higher VEGF concentrations in malignant ascites than in non-malignant (cirrhotic, tuberculous, inflammatory) ascites. Although VEGF concentrations are significantly higher in malignant ascites, the overlap in the concentrations of VEGF between malignant and non-malignant ascites is rather large. For example, relative to non-malignant ascites, when using its VEGF mean levels 119.44 pg/ml (70.90±48.54) as the minimum cut-off limit, the sensitivity and specificity of VEGF to diagnose malignant ascites were 91.3% and 90.9%, respectively. Nascimento et al. and Bamias et al. used 662 pg/ml and 400 pg/ml as cut-off values to discriminate between malignant ascites and non-malignant ascites, respectively.

tree.case_summary:
A 57-year-old man presents to the emergency department with several days of malaise, weakness, and night sweats. Today, he experienced a headache with blurry vision, thus prompting his presentation. The patient has a history of diabetes and is followed closely by an endocrinologist. Otherwise, he has lost 10 pounds over the past month. His temperature is 100°F (37.8°C), blood pressure is 122/90 mmHg, pulse is 84/min, respirations are 16/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Physical exam is notable for a thin man but is otherwise unremarkable. His visual acuity is 20/100 in both eyes, though he says that he normally has 20/20 vision. His gait is mildly ataxic as well, but his neurological exam is otherwise nonfocal. Laboratory studies are ordered as seen below.

Hemoglobin: 10 g/dL
Hematocrit: 31%
Leukocyte count: 57,500/mm^3 with 35% blasts
Platelet count: 109,000/mm^3

Serum:
Na+: 139 mEq/L
Cl-: 100 mEq/L
K+: 4.1 Eq/L
HCO3-: 22 mEq/L
BUN: 20 mg/dL
Glucose: 99 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.1 mg/dL
Calcium: 10.0 mEq/L

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
B. Acute myelogenous leukemia
C. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
D. Chronic myelogenous leukemia
E. Multiple myeloma

excluded_candidates: Diabetes complication: reason ranked lower due to presence of systemic symptoms and leukocytosis with blasts
Infection: reason ranked lower due to lack of clear infectious symptoms and presence of systemic findings
